q: Define residual sugar and give the approximate threshold at which most palates first detect sweetness.
accept: sugar left after fermentation about 4-9 g/l
ans: Sugar remaining after fermentation; most detect it around 4–9 g/L, depending on acidity
exp: High acid masks sugar — a Mosel Kabinett at 40 g/L can read off-dry.

q: What is pH's practical significance in winemaking, and the typical range for quality wine?
ans: ~3.0–3.8; lower pH means better microbial stability, brighter color and more effective SO2
exp: High-pH wines need more sulfur and spoil faster — the warm-vintage problem in one number.

accept: ta is all acids va is acetic
total is all acids volatile is steam distillable
ans: TA measures all acids (chiefly tartaric/malic); VA measures the steam-distillable ones — essentially acetic acid
exp: TA is structure; VA above threshold is a fault.

q: What is the legal and sensory definition of 'dry' for still wine in the EU?
accept: up to 4 g/l or 9 with acidity
ans: ≤4 g/L residual sugar (or ≤9 g/L if TA is within 2 g/L of the sugar)
exp: The acidity allowance is why some 'dry' wines carry noticeable sugar.

q: Explain how alcohol contributes to perceived sweetness and body.
accept: ethanol tastes slightly sweet adds viscosity weight
alcohol gives body and sweet impression
ans: Ethanol reads faintly sweet and adds viscosity — high-alcohol dry wines can seem sweeter and always seem fuller
exp: Why a 15% Zinfandel is called 'jammy' when it is technically bone dry.

q: Name the three classes of wine aroma by origin.
exp: Naming the class before the descriptor is the deductive habit examiners reward.

q: Which structural component most reliably signals climate in a blind glass?
exp: Acid falls as ripening advances — high acid points cool, low acid points warm, more consistently than anything else.

q: Explain what a wine's 'finish' actually measures.
accept: persistence of flavor after swallowing seconds
ans: The persistence of flavor after the wine leaves the palate, measured in seconds — the fastest honest quality marker
exp: Distinguish length from mere heat or bitterness lingering.

q: Mousy taint hides from the nose because the compounds responsible:
opts: Are non-volatile at the wine's own pH
Bind irreversibly to tannin in the bottle
Sit below the detection threshold in wine
Volatilize only above 20°C in the glass
exp: The culprits are nitrogen heterocycles — 2-acetyltetrahydropyridine and its relatives — produced by Brettanomyces and by lactic acid bacteria. At wine pH they are protonated and effectively non-volatile, so the glass smells clean; saliva at near-neutral pH deprotonates them in the mouth, the free base volatilizes retronasally, and you get that lingering popcorn, stale rice-cake, rodent-cage aftertaste that builds rather than fades. Hence the technique: taste, swallow or spit, then wait several seconds before judging. The fault has become common again because it thrives in low-SO2, higher-pH wines, and sensitivity varies so widely that some tasters cannot perceive it at all.

q: A négociant-éleveur differs from a courtier in that they:
accept: buy and raise wine vs broker
ans: Take ownership and 'raise' (élevage) wine for sale; the courtier merely brokers between parties
exp: Élevage — upbringing — is the untranslatable middle of the trade.

q: 'La Place de Bordeaux' now also distributes which non-Bordeaux icons (name one)?
ans: e.g., Opus One, Masseto, Almaviva, Seña — September's 'hors Bordeaux' campaign
exp: The old merchant network became a global luxury channel.

q: Provenance vocabulary: 'ullage: base neck' on an auction lot means:
accept: fill level at base of neck excellent
ans: Fill to the base of the neck — excellent for mature wine
exp: Top/mid/low shoulder descend the worry ladder; 'ex-château' trumps all.

q: Why does a magnum age more slowly than a 750?
ans: Similar oxygen ingress serves double the wine — slower maturation per liter

q: The chemical family formed as tannins and anthocyanins link during aging:
ans: Polymeric pigments — color stabilizes brick-ward, tannins soften, sediment forms
exp: Why old red stains less and tastes silkier.
